The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?

Where things stand

The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.

What to do next

Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. In your defence to counterclaim, you must admit every fact in the counterclaim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is taken as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. If the counterclaim is for damages, the amount stays in dispute unless you specifically admit it. If you plan to prove a different version of the facts, denying theirs is not enough. You must set out your own version. You must also set out any point you will rely on to defeat the counterclaim, if it might take the defendant by surprise or raise a new issue. If the 20 days pass, you may still deliver your defence to counterclaim at any time before you are noted in default.

Your deadline

Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.

The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?

Where things stand

The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.

What to do next

Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. In your defence to counterclaim, you must admit every fact in the counterclaim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is taken as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. If the counterclaim is for damages, the amount stays in dispute unless you specifically admit it. If you plan to prove a different version of the facts, denying theirs is not enough. You must set out your own version. You must also set out any point you will rely on to defeat the counterclaim, if it might take the defendant by surprise or raise a new issue. If the 20 days pass, you may still deliver your defence to counterclaim at any time before you are noted in default.

Your deadline

Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.

The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?

Where things stand

The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.

What to do next

Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. In your defence to counterclaim, you must admit every fact in the counterclaim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is taken as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. If the counterclaim is for damages, the amount stays in dispute unless you specifically admit it. If you plan to prove a different version of the facts, denying theirs is not enough. You must set out your own version. You must also set out any point you will rely on to defeat the counterclaim, if it might take the defendant by surprise or raise a new issue. If the 20 days pass, you may still deliver your defence to counterclaim at any time before you are noted in default.

Your deadline

Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.

What it costs

Filing a defence (no fee if you already paid for a notice of intent to defend): $194
O. Reg. 293/92 (Superior Court of Justice and Court of Appeal fees), s. 1 (1), para. 3 ii · checked 2026-09-30

“If no notice of intent to defend has been filed by the same party, a statement of defence, a defence to counterclaim, a defence to crossclaim or a third party defence, $194.”

If you cannot afford the fee, you can ask the court to waive it. Asking costs nothing.
ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived, Overview · checked 2026-09-27

“If you cannot afford to pay the fees, you can ask the court to waive them. ... There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.”

Where and how to file

In the Toronto region, file online through the Ontario Courts Public Portal.
ontario.ca, File a civil claim online, Overview · checked 2026-09-27

“Starting October 14, 2025, all online filings for the Toronto region must be submitted using the Ontario Courts Public Portal.”

Outside Toronto, file online through the Civil Claims Online or Civil Submissions Online portal.
ontario.ca, File a civil claim online, Overview · checked 2026-09-27

“The Civil Claims Online and Civil Submissions Online portals will continue to be available to file court documents online for civil and Divisional Court cases in other regions outside of Toronto.”

If a deadline is 3 business days away or fewer, you cannot file online for it.
ontario.ca, File a civil claim online, Documents you can file online · checked 2026-09-27

“if you need to meet a deadline established by legislation or other court rules, court practice direction or a court order that is 3 business days or fewer away”

Serving it on the other side

Other documents go to the other side's lawyer if they have one; a person acting for themselves can be served by mail to their last address for service.
Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 16.01 (4) · checked 2026-09-27

“shall be served on a party who has a lawyer of record by serving the lawyer, and service may be made in a manner provided in rule 16.05; (b) may be served on a party acting in person or on a person who is not a party, (i) by mailing a copy of the document to the last address for service provided by the party or other person or, if no such address has been provided, to the party's or person's last known address”

Prove service with an affidavit of service (Form 16B) from whoever served it.
Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 16.09 (1) · checked 2026-09-27

“Service of a document may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).”

The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?

Where things stand

The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.

What to do next

Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. Your deadline

Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.
